1.pericope_label: And it came to pass after these things, that Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard, which was in Jezreel, hard by the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. And Ahab spake unto Naboth, saying, Give me thy vineyard, that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near unto my house: and I will give thee for it a better vineyard than it; or, if it seem good to thee, I will give thee the worth of it in money. And Naboth said to Ahab, The Lord forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee. And Ahab came into his house heavy and displeased because of the word which Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him: for he had said, I will not give thee the inheritance of my fathers. And he laid him down upon his bed, and turned away his face, and would eat no bread.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch infer from the title king of Samaria that Jezreel, the modern Zerin, was only a summer residence, and hold that Naboth was not merely free to refuse the sale but bound to refuse it, the alienation of a patrimony being forbidden by the law. Ellicott opens the location as a genuine question: the Septuagint drops the words which was in Jezreel and puts the ground beside a threshing-floor at Samaria, and he weighs the emphatic prediction of the nineteenth verse, its fulfilment at the pool of Samaria, and the apparent setting of the action there against the received reading, the plainer sense of his city, and the plot of ground at Jezreel in Second Kings. He judges Samaria the likelier without claiming the difficulty can be cleared up, and reads the whole scene as true to nature, finding in the refusal a certain harshness and in the sulk the seedplot of crime.

Gill dates the coveting after the two Syrian campaigns, in which Ahab conquered and then released the blasphemer Benhadad. He takes the herb garden for a kitchen plot or a flower garden or with Kimchi both, and traces the taste to the Syrians, whose horticulture Pliny praised; on the refusal he notes that Naboth was prosperous and under no compulsion to sell, counts him among the seven thousand who never bowed to Baal, and suspects the crown already bore him a grudge.

Clarke records that the Septuagint transposes this chapter and the one before it, so that the murder precedes the Syrian war, and that Josephus keeps the same order. On the law he insists no Israelite could finally alienate a paternal inheritance, so that the request was itself a temptation to sin and high iniquity in the king; he adds that despotic as these monarchs were none dared simply seize a field, since the constitution they administered as vicegerents of God gave them no power to alter an old statute or frame a new one. Of the sulk he says only that a man lord of ten-twelfths of the land was made wretched for want of one poor plot.

Henry reads possession itself as the snare and nearness to greatness as the danger. Desiring a convenience is no sin, but inordinate desire breaks the tenth commandment even when pursued by lawful means; Canaan was peculiarly God's own country and Israel his tenants, so that Naboth could not sell, and Henry reports the conjecture that he held his acre as an earnest of the heavenly portion. He notes the irony that Ahab, having let slip the chance to enlarge his realm after beating the Syrians, now strains to enlarge a garden, and finds discontent both its own punishment and its own parent, since Paul was content in a prison and this king miserable in a palace.

debates.question: Where did Naboth vineyard lie, at Jezreel or near Samaria?

positions.position: Near Samaria, on the whole the more probable, since the sentence of verse 19 was fulfilled at that city pool and the action of the chapter seems to happen there
At Jezreel, as the received text, the phrase his city, and the plot of ground in Second Kings imply
At Jezreel, which the title king of Samaria shows to have been a summer residence only

5.pericope_label: But Jezebel his wife came to him, and said unto him, Why is thy spirit so sad, that thou eatest no bread? And he said unto her, Because I spake unto Naboth the Jezreelite, and said unto him, Give me thy vineyard for money; or else, if it please thee, I will give thee another vineyard for it: and he answered, I will not give thee my vineyard. And Jezebel his wife said unto him, Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel? arise, and eat bread, and let thine heart be merry: I will give thee the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite. So she wrote letters in Ahab’s name, and sealed them with his seal, and sent the letters unto the elders and to the nobles that were in his city, dwelling with Naboth. And she wrote in the letters, saying, Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people: And set two men, sons of Belial, before him, to bear witness against him, saying, Thou didst blaspheme God and the king. And then carry him out, and stone him, that he may die.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the queen question as irony, the pronoun thrown forward for emphasis and the Greek taking it interrogatively, and describe the signet as a seal bearing the royal name and stamped rather than signed, as is still done among Arabs, Turks and Persians, which gave a letter the force of a command. Ellicott compares the scorn to the impatience of Lady Macbeth and finds in the invitation to eat and be merry a half-contemptuous reading of the same self-indulgence Elijah had played upon earlier; he argues that the seal, being carried on the person, implies the king knew something was being done in his name and took care not to ask what, and he treats the fast as more than disguise, a hint of hidden guilt that prepares the accusation. On the charge he renders the verb as renounce rather than blaspheme, though stoning followed as for blasphemy proper.

Gill has Jezebel simply noticing her husband low spirits and wishing to relieve them, and assumes the seal was lent without the scheme being disclosed. He reports Kimchi reading of proclaim a fast as convene a court and prefers it, on the ground that Jezebel can have had little notion of fasting and that a genuine humiliation would hardly be cried in one town only; the two witnesses he calls men who had thrown off the yoke of the law and would swear to anything.

Clarke says flatly that she counterfeited the royal authority by its owner consent, and reduces the taunt to a maxim: if Naboth may refuse and Ahab may not take, Naboth is the greater man of the two, and this is the native speech of despotism. On the indictment he reports Parkhurst contention that the verb never means to curse, so that the accusation ran rather that Naboth had blessed the false gods, a capital matter under Deuteronomy; he prefers the plainer sense and warns that letting a single word carry two opposite meanings is dangerous.

Henry treats the comfort as a pretence for feeding pride and blowing the coals of corruption, and fastens on the misreport, since Naboth said he may not sell and the king repeated it as he will not, turning conscience into peevishness. He allows the taunt a good sense as well as a bad one, then presses the wickedness of the orders themselves, which required the magistrates to find the witnesses, suborn them, and judge on evidence known to be false. Religion was made the cover, and he concludes that no wickedness is so vile that religion has not at some time been used to hide it, nor any so monstrous as one carried through with the forms of law; he also explains why both God and king stand in the charge, since profaning the one cost a man his life and treason against the other cost him his land.

debates.question: What did the order to proclaim a fast mean?

A genuine fast, implying that some hidden offence had drawn danger on the city, and so preparing the way for the accusation

11.pericope_label: And the men of his city, even the elders and the nobles who were the inhabitants in his city, did as Jezebel had sent unto them, and as it was written in the letters which she had sent unto them. They proclaimed a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people. And there came in two men, children of Belial, and sat before him: and the men of Belial witnessed against him, even against Naboth, in the presence of the people, saying, Naboth did blaspheme God and the king. Then they carried him forth out of the city, and stoned him with stones, that he died. Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, Naboth is stoned, and is dead. And it came to pass, when Jezebel heard that Naboth was stoned, and was dead, that Jezebel said to Ahab, Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give thee for money: for Naboth is not alive, but dead. And it came to pass, when Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, that Ahab rose up to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the compliance of the magistrates as typical of the baser forms of organised Eastern despotism, which will not take life by open violence without some cause shown yet can always poison the springs of justice, and adds a reason peculiar to Israel, that where the crown was reckoned only the deputy of God and subject in theory to the supreme law, crime would especially need legal clothing. On the carrying out of the city he gives the usual reason, that blood must not pollute the place, and raises the possibility that the stoning happened on the dead man own ground. He holds that with the sons killed there was no claimant, and that a traitor property would naturally fall to the crown although the Law enacts nothing of the kind; the Greek insertion about rending the clothes he judges poorly attested and probably drawn back from the later verse. Keil and Delitzsch supply the missing principle, that as a blasphemer goods were forfeited to the Lord as cherem, so a traitor goods were held forfeit to the king.

Gill is surprised less by the queen invention, or by the presence of men who would swear to anything, than by the magistrates themselves, and concludes that idolatry once prevailing strips away every sense of humanity and justice. He reads the posture of the two hirelings as significant, since accuser and accused sat facing one another as they later did among the Romans, and notes that Josephus makes the witnesses three while the Targum and every ancient version keep them at two.

Clarke infers from the divine complaint about the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons that the whole family was destroyed, so that the ground escheated with no heir at law, and admits that by what rites possession was taken nobody now knows.

Henry observes that the elders neither raised a difficulty nor met with one, whether from fear of the queen or hatred of the man piety, and offers both titles to the land in turn, failure of blood if the sons were dead and forfeiture by crime if they were not, with the queen will to serve if neither would. He notes that the king went himself rather than sending an officer, and went in state, since Jehu remembered long afterwards riding behind him that day; and he sets one symmetry beside another, orders from Samaria to the elders of Jezreel murdering Naboth and orders later from Jezreel to the elders of Samaria murdering the seventy sons of Ahab, so that rulers who debauch the consciences of their magistrates may find the wheel come round.

debates.question: How many witnesses appeared against Naboth?

positions.position: Three, according to Josephus
Two, as the Targum and every ancient version have it

debates.question: On what title did the vineyard pass to the crown?

positions.position: By a principle implied in the idea of treason, since a blasphemer goods were cherem to the Lord and a traitor goods forfeit to the king, though no Mosaic rule says so
By escheat, the whole family having been destroyed so that no heir at law remained
By failure of blood if the sons died, by forfeiture for crime if they did not, and failing both by the naked will of Jezebel

17.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, which is in Samaria: behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, whither he is gone down to possess it. And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the Lord, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the Lord, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine. And Ahab said to Elijah, Hast thou found me, O mine enemy? And he answered, I have found thee: because thou hast sold thyself to work evil in the sight of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the prophet long absence deliberate, since the merely political business of the preceding chapter drew him out not at all and he returns for the higher duty of rebuking crime and avenging blood that Eastern tyranny would think a trifle. He holds the words about Samaria almost meaningless unless they say the king was then in that city, and calls any softening of them an explaining away; he admires the brevity of the accusation, which shames the attempt to shift everything onto Jezebel and leaves its object speechless, and he rejects outright any fulfilment of the sentence in the fate of Jehoram, arguing that the emphasis of even thy blood forbids it and that the later reprieve touches a different clause of the doom. Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase instead as who dwells in Samaria, since the king was plainly at Jezreel when the prophet met him, and reject the Vulgate and Luther rendering of the greeting for the plainer dost thou meet me again, explaining the epithet as an attempt to blunt the threat by making it look like private spite.

Gill admits that nobody knows where Elijah had been since the call of Elisha or at what, and guesses that during the Syrian war he was founding or reviving the schools of the prophets whose pupils appear later; the Targum names the message the word of prophecy. He notes that the Vulgate and the Arabic, with Joseph Kimchi and Ben Melech, read the accusation flat rather than as a question, and that the killing is laid at the king door because his coveting caused it, his wife contrived it, and he very likely knew and consented to more than the record says. The title enemy he explains simply, that the prophet dealt faithfully and reproved him.

Clarke dates the meeting to the day after the killing, reasoning back from the divine complaint in Second Kings. He holds it vain to look for a literal fulfilment of the sentence, since the penitence of the last verse deferred the stroke: dogs licked this king blood at the pool of Samaria where his chariot was washed after Ramoth-gilead, though some make that the very spot of the stoning, while the word touching his son came true to the letter when the body of Jehoram was flung into the ground of Naboth. He glosses the selling of oneself from Paul and compares Orestes sending Aegisthus to die where he had killed.

Henry sets the two errands side by side, a prophet of lower rank sent to Ahab with kindness before the battle and the father of the prophets sent now to convict him of murder, and dwells on the staging, since sentence is read in the vineyard itself at the moment of entry, because entering avowed the whole business and made the king an accessory after the fact. He closes off the evasions, that the law killed Naboth and that the prosecution was none of the king doing, with the rule that the land passes with its encumbrance; and he sharpens the comparison with Paul, who was sold under sin as a captive against his will, whereas this man made the sale himself and of choice.

positions.position: Not literally of Ahab, since repentance deferred it; the blood was licked at the pool of Samaria, and the word touching the son came true when Jehoram body was cast into the ground of Naboth
Literally and of Ahab himself, since the emphasis of even thy blood forbids transferring it to Jehoram, and the deferral of verse 29 touches another clause

21.pericope_label: Behold, I will bring evil upon thee, and will take away thy posterity, and will cut off from Ahab him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel, And will make thine house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah, for the provocation wherewith thou hast provoked me to anger, and made Israel to sin. And of Jezebel also spake the Lord, saying, The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel. Him that dieth of Ahab in the city the dogs shall eat; and him that dieth in the field shall the fowls of the air eat. But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the Lord, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up. And he did very abominably in following idols, according to all things as did the Amorites, whom the Lord cast out before the children of Israel.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the doom out as one continuous oracle and mark the point where the historian own reflection begins. Ellicott makes much of the delay in naming the instigator, since throughout the rebuke the prophet has disdained to mention the woman onto whom the coward had shifted everything, leaving the king exposed as the responsible party; the sentence against her is a doom of shame that rarely falls on a woman but fits one who has forsworn the pity and modesty of her sex, her body thrown as offal into the ditch beyond the wall where refuse draws the half-wild scavengers of an Eastern town. In the closing comment he finds contempt as much as condemnation, for a most unkingly king who sold himself to a course of crime he was half unwilling to take, against a conscience he did not disbelieve but ignored, and for a paltry want, and who grovelled besides under the open rule of a wife; and he reads the comparison with the Amorites as reaching past false worship to the practices that always attended it.

Gill hears the first clause of the doom as personal, a violent end for the king himself, and notes the bitterness of that in a man with seventy sons to carry his name. He recalls that the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha were rooted out entirely, so that the comparison is no vague one, and reads the promise of dogs and birds as meaning simply that none of them will be buried; the idols followed he renders dunghill gods, after the Tigurine version.

Clarke reports the fulfilment of the sentence on Jezebel as exact, and remarks that the bodies of poor Hindoos, and of those who have suffered public punishment, are still thrown into the rivers and eaten at the banks by dogs, vultures and crows. Of the king he says the man hired himself out to the devil and laboured at the work, and of the wife who stirred him up that a good wife is from the Lord and a bad one from the devil.

Henry first closes off the two escapes, that the law killed Naboth, since perverted justice is the worst injustice of all, and that the prosecution was none of the king doing, since it was done to please him and he showed himself pleased: he killed, because he took possession, and whoever takes the garden takes the guilt with it. He supplies the precedents for the curse, the same terms having been spoken already against Jeroboam and Baasha, observes how much of the sentence concerns the body after death and wonders whether such penalties figure a worse misery for the soul, and weighs this verdict against another, since what was done to Uriah resembled it closely yet David in that one matter excepted did what was right, while here the severity answers not to the vineyard alone but to a life of idolatry.

outliers.claim: Illustrates the fate of Jezebel from present practice among the Hindoos, whose poor and publicly executed are thrown into the rivers and devoured at the banks by dogs, vultures and crows

27.pericope_label: And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly. And the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? because he humbleth himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days: but in his son’s days will I bring the evil upon his house.

schools.summary: Ellicott surveys the versions on the closing phrase and judges the Eastern renderings and Josephus, with their barefoot, far the most probable, while noting that some Greek copies and the Latin give a bowed head instead. On the repentance he holds the two halves together: the outburst is exactly what an impressible temper would produce and might fairly be despised as too late and as the child of fear, more alive to the shame of discovery than to the shamefulness of the deed, yet God finds in its very imperfection some germ of promise, and the partial remission proves the notice taken, so that the king still meets the end foretold but dies in honour while the ruin of the house waits for his son. Keil and Delitzsch call the remorse neither hypocritical nor merely outward but sincere, though neither lasting nor productive of any real conversion, and rest that judgment on the Lord own acknowledgement of it.

Gill reports the Jewish tradition generously, that the king prayed and fasted morning and evening, studied the law all his remaining days, never returned to his old works and was truly converted, and then dismantles it: the queen is never rebuked for the murder, the vineyard is never restored to the family, the idols stay, and within a chapter the same man is consulting four hundred prophets of the groves and saying plainly that he hates the one true prophet. What moved him was dread of punishment rather than fear of God, and yet Gill concedes that nothing like it had been seen in any of his wicked predecessors and that heaven took notice.

Clarke walks through the torn clothes, the hair garment next the skin, the fast and the nights in sackcloth and reads each as unfeigned; on the last phrase he prefers the sense of going unshod, following Jarchi and the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic against the Vulgate hanging head and the rendering went groaning, and he hears in the slow measured tread the note Aeschylus struck over the defeat of Xerxes. He will allow no doubt about the repentance, since the divine approval settles it, and holds that any measure of godly sorrow meets a proportionate regard from the Father of compassion.

Henry calls him a kind of penitent, granting the fact and refusing the substance: a proud hardened sinner was genuinely reduced, for God can make the stoutest heart tremble, but this was the dress and bearing of repentance, the garments torn and not the heart, and a hypocrite may travel far in the outward performance of holy duty and still fall short. The reprieve he treats as a kind of pardon rather than a reversal, the sentence standing and only its execution put off to the son, and he takes the mercy shown to such a man as evidence of a readiness to forgive in which, as Bishop Sanderson put it, God would sooner be thought unholy or untrue or unjust than unmerciful.

debates.question: Was the repentance of Ahab sincere?

positions.position: Genuine and unfeigned, the divine approval putting it beyond doubt
Sincere though neither lasting nor productive of conversion, since the Lord himself called it a humbling
External only and moved by dread of punishment rather than fear of God, as the unrebuked queen, the unrestored vineyard and the retained idols show
The dress and bearing of repentance without the heart, yet enough to earn a reprieve because it gave God some glory
Imperfect and born of fear, despicable to human judgment, yet holding some germ of promise that God did not disregard
